header:
Date: 2026-07-08
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Citrine Head of ML), Tom Reyes (Citrine CTO), Lena Ortiz (Citrine DevOps)
Recording: yes
Notes: discovery focused on per-token unit economics, batching/caching levers, and hosting choices (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
summary: Citrine Analytics is evaluating tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployment options. Primary drivers: strict monthly budget, need for sub-150ms p50 for short chat flows, and data residency requirements for a subset of customer prompts. They want a quick pilot to measure unit cost with batching and KV/prefix caching and to understand fixed committed costs for Dedicated. Security is a gating item for Private; SOC2 and KMS integration were discussed. Next steps: pricing spreadsheet, benchmark run, share prompts, and follow-up on networking constraints.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (cost, latency, commitments)
Security: SOC 2, SSO, KMS, audit logs
transcript:
[00:00:00] Alicia: okay everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off. I'm Alicia from Redwood, account exec. Marcus is our solutions engineer. 
[00:00:09] Marcus: hey all. thanks. real quick agenda: understand your workload, cost targets, and constraints then talk through hosting options and levers like batching/caching.
[00:00:22] Priya: cool yeah we're replacing a prototype that runs locally, and cost is the main blocker for scaling. we have chat flows and a few high-throughput ranking jobs.
[00:00:31] Tom: and to add, we need sub-150ms p50 for the support chat use-case for good UX. p95 can be higher but p50 is important.
[00:00:40] Lena: also some customers require that certain PII prompts never leave their region, so residency is a thing.
[00:00:48] Marcus: got it. does that mean some traffic could be routed to a Private/VPC-only model while the rest goes to hosted?
[00:00:54] Priya: yep, that's the idea. we'll likely slice traffic by sensitivity and maybe by feature flag.
[00:01:02] Alicia: just to ground this, what's your current monthly budget for inference ops? ballpark.
[00:01:08] Priya: we can commit roughly $18k/month for now. if unit costs are low and predictability is better we could expand.
[00:01:14] Marcus: perfect, that's useful. one high-level note: per-token price times tokens plus fixed committed costs for Dedicated add up; we can model both. are you optimizing for cost per dialog or cost per 1k QPS?
[00:01:28] Tom: per dialog, primarily. we care about latency too but dialogs are the billing unit for product economics.
[00:01:34] Marcus: okay. a couple levers we commonly use: (1) batching — run many short requests together to amortize GPU work; (2) prefix or KV caching — for repeated system prompts or reused prefixes; (3) quantized model variants that reduce cost but could change quality slightly.
[00:01:52] Priya: can you say more about caching? we have a lot of repeated system text across sessions.
[00:01:56] Marcus: sure. prefix caching stores token-level key/value state for common prefixes so we don't recompute the same attention results. it works especially well if the conversation starts with standard onboarding text or known templates. we sometimes call it KV cache but transcription might say K-V cash. (laugh)
[00:02:15] Priya: (laugh) note taken. how much savings are realistic?
[00:02:19] Marcus: depends on repetition and sequence length. in our baseline examples we see 20–60% token compute reduction when 30–40% of requests reuse prefixes. batching can be 2–4x efficiency uplift for short inputs if you can tolerate slightly higher p95.
[00:02:34] Tom: what do you mean by tolerate p95? our SLA is client-facing.
[00:02:39] Marcus: p95 increases because batching holds requests up until batch fills or until a latency deadline. Redwood has dynamic batch sizing — so you'll get a configurable latency cap. say p50 120ms and p95 280ms in a batched config vs p50 80ms p95 220ms in a lower batch size.
[00:02:58] Lena: okay and Dedicated changes that how?
[00:03:02] Marcus: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity so batching becomes more predictable — you don't compete with multi-tenant spikes. unit cost per token can drop because you run larger, more efficient batches and can use slightly more aggressive quantization safely. but there's a commit — e.g., a monthly reserved instance charge.
[00:03:19] Alicia: to put numbers on the table, for a medium open-chat model we list hosted per-token at, uh, $0.00035 per output token (example), and Dedicated effective unit might be closer to $0.00020 when amortizing reserved capacity and using batching/caching. these are sample numbers — we'll send exact spreadsheets.
[00:03:38] Priya: that differential matters. if our typical dialog is 120 output tokens, that multiplies.
[00:03:44] Marcus: exactly. 120 tokens at $0.00035 is about $0.042 per dialog. at $0.00020 it's $0.024. at 50k dialogs/month that's a big delta.
[00:03:56] Tom: what's the break-even for Dedicated reservation vs hosted?
[00:04:00] Marcus: depends on utilization. rough rule of thumb: if you're sustaining >60–70% of a Dedicated pool across the month and need predictable latency, Dedicated often pays off. but if you're spiky and underutilized, hosted can be cheaper. we'll model your expected QPS and dialogs in the spreadsheet.
[00:04:16] Priya: our traffic is moderate but with big spikes around daytime support hours. can Redwood do burst capacity?
[00:04:23] Marcus: yes, Dedicated has burst options — configurable. burst is priced as added temporary capacity or overage per minute depending on contract.
[00:04:31] Priya: and Private — that's the VPC/on-prem offering — how different is unit pricing?
[00:04:36] Alicia: Private has a platform fee and often a higher per-token cost if we manage the infra, but if you run on-prem with your hardware, the unit compute is basically your infra cost. Redwood charges for the control plane and any managed services like caching etc. Security integrations (KMS, HSM) are add-ons in terms of setup complexity.
[00:04:54] Tom: we have HSM and strict KMS requirements. is Redwood's private offering certified to plug into our KMS?
[00:05:00] Marcus: yes, we integrate with customer-managed KMS, and we have SOC2 compliance docs. for on-prem there's an extra ops runbook. we'll share the SOC2 summary and private deployment checklist.
[00:05:11] Lena: network wise, will we need specific egress ports or can it be fully contained?
[00:05:15] Marcus: for a VPC deployment, control plane calls home for management but data paths can be kept in-region and encrypted. we have an air-gapped package for very strict customers, but that adds onboarding time.
[00:05:26] Priya: onboarding time — how long to get to pilot?
[00:05:29] Alicia: for hosted it's minutes — you can start calling the API. for a pilot with integrations, benchmark and validation, typical timeline is 2–4 weeks. Dedicated onboarding is 3–6 weeks depending on networking and compliance. Private/on-prem can be 6–12 weeks based on ops windows.
[00:05:44] Tom: 6–12 is long but acceptable if security needs it.
[00:05:47] Marcus: quick note on benchmarking: we prefer you provide a sample prompt set and representative QPS. we'll run throughput tests with a matching model/quantization and show cost/latency breakdowns.
[00:05:59] Priya: we can do that. we'll provide three use-cases: support chat (short), document summarization (longer), and reranking (high QPS).
[00:06:08] Marcus: perfect. reranking is important — batching there looks different: many short scoring requests, often benefited by specialized batchers and sometimes smaller quantized models.
[00:06:18] Tom: one more question: are you able to do model pinning and rollbacks if a new model version has regressions?
[00:06:23] Marcus: yes — we have version pinning and rollout policies (canary, A/B). Optimize has eval monitoring so you can detect quality regressions on your prompt set.
[00:06:33] Priya: about cost modeling: can you include caching assumptions in the spreadsheet? we need to see sensitivity: 0%, 25%, 50% cache hit.
[00:06:40] Alicia: absolutely. we'll include scenarios for cache hit rates and batch sizes. Marcus will annotate assumptions for token counts and latencies.
[00:06:48] Marcus: also worth noting tokenization mismatch risk — different models tokenize differently; we'll use your actual token counts in the benchmark. sometimes the inference token count differs from naive estimates.
[00:06:59] Priya: good call. expectations: we want a pilot to show per-dialog cost below $0.03 while keeping p50 <150ms for chat.
[00:07:09] Tom: and show a path to lowering cost to $0.02 with Dedicated and caching.
[00:07:14] Marcus: that's achievable on paper. we'll run numbers.
[00:07:17] Alicia: any legal or procurement items we should prep for?
[00:07:20] Tom: standard NDA is already done. procurement will want a SOW for the pilot and a sample contract.
[00:07:25] Alicia: we'll attach a pilot SOW.
[00:07:28] Lena: connectivity question: our dev cluster sits behind strict firewall rules. will Redwood need open egress to management plane?
[00:07:34] Marcus: for VPC deployments there's a management control channel; we can provide IP ranges and set up peering or private link depending on cloud. for on-prem we'll need some ops coordination.
[00:07:45] Priya: any known gotchas around mem use with long-context summarization?
[00:07:49] Marcus: long contexts increase KV memory but you can shard and stream; we have memory tuning knobs. for heavy summarization we recommend a model that supports larger context tokens and potentially chunking + retrieval to bound cost.
[00:08:03] Priya: okay. a couple of side questions I jotted down: will Redwood provide rate-limited endpoints and token-level usage breakdowns?
[00:08:10] Alicia: yes — console has token-level breakdowns by route and model, and you can set quotas/limits.
[00:08:15] Tom: what about data retention for logs and transcripts? our policy is 90 days then purge.
[00:08:20] Marcus: you can configure retention windows; down to zero retention in Private modes. Hosted has default retention and options for shorter retention with enterprise plans. we'll include that in the security doc.
[00:08:33] Priya: earlier Marcus said 20–60% savings from caching in some cases — how conservative should we be for modeling?
[00:08:38] Marcus: start conservative: model 20% cache hit for baseline, and a 40–50% optimistic case. we'll show both.
[00:08:45] Speaker 1: (inaudible mutter)
[00:08:49] Alicia: let's recap next steps. We'll send the pricing sheet and unit-econ model with scenarios for cache hits and batch sizes; Marcus will schedule benchmarks once you share prompts; Priya will share the prompt sets and expected QPS; Lena will confirm networking constraints for VPC.
[00:09:05] Priya: yep, we'll do that. thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[00:09:10] Alicia: great. I'll follow up with the spreadsheet and SOC2 summary; Marcus will ping about available benchmark windows.
[00:09:17] Tom: thanks all.
[00:09:19] Marcus: thanks. end.
[00:09:22] (end recording)

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker overlaps and occasional transcription errors (e.g., KV cache transcribed as K-V cash).
